Assume energies are measured relative to the rest masses, as appropriate for the nonrelativistic Hamiltonian. Let the lattice have L sites in each direction, spacing a, and physical side length L_phy = La.

(a) Single-particle basis and spin singlets

For f = n,p and s = ↑,↓, let a†_{rfs} create a nucleon of flavor f and spin s at site r. The periodic plane-wave creation operator and one-particle basis state are

a†_{kfs} = L^(−3/2) Σ_r exp(ik·r) a†_{rfs},    |k,f,s⟩ = a†_{kfs}|0⟩,

where k_i = 2πm_i/L_phy, with m_i chosen from the lattice momentum range. The states are orthonormal with the usual fermionic anticommutation relations.

For distinct momentum orbitals k and q, examples of normalized spin-singlet states are

|nn;k,q;S=0⟩ = [n†_{k↑}n†_{q↓} − n†_{k↓}n†_{q↑}]|0⟩/√2,

|pp;k,q;S=0⟩ = [p†_{k↑}p†_{q↓} − p†_{k↓}p†_{q↑}]|0⟩/√2,

|np;k,q;S=0⟩ = [n†_{k↑}p†_{q↓} − n†_{k↓}p†_{q↑}]|0⟩/√2.

The first two describe identical nucleons; the third specifies a neutron in orbital k and a proton in orbital q. For two identical nucleons in the same momentum orbital, the normalized nn state is n†_{k↑}n†_{k↓}|0⟩, and likewise for pp. The distinct-orbital formula should not be used at k=q for identical particles, since its two terms then give the same state up to fermionic reordering.

(b) Matching the lattice hopping parameter

Fourier transforming the free lattice Hamiltonian gives the single-particle dispersion

ε(k) = 2t Σ_{i=1}^3 [1 − cos(k_i a)].

The literal lowest mode is k=0, with ε(0)=0 for every t; matching that mode cannot determine t. The calibration must therefore use the lowest nonzero momentum mode, with one component k_i=2π/L_phy and the other two zero. Its lattice energy is

ε₁ = 2t[1 − cos(2π/L)] = 4t sin²(π/L).

For a nonrelativistic particle of mass M_phy in the periodic physical box, the corresponding energy above rest is (2π/L_phy)²/(2M_phy). Equating the two gives the exact finite-L matching result

t = π²/[2M_phy L_phy² sin²(π/L)].

In the continuum limit, a=L_phy/L and sin(π/L) ≈ π/L, so this becomes t ≈ 1/(2M_phy a²), the usual continuum hopping scale.

(c) Lowest nonzero single-particle energy

Using ħc = 197.32698 MeV·fm, the energy of the lowest nonzero mode is

ε₁ = [2π(ħc)/L_phy]²/(2M_phy)
    = [2π(197.32698 MeV·fm)/(3.4 fm)]²/(2·1634 MeV)
    ≈ 40.7 MeV.

(d) Bound state, coupling, and the first excitation

Let B=17.8 MeV, so that the bound-state energy is −B. At fixed lattice spacing, write the on-site interaction strength as U=Ct. For a zero-total-momentum pair, the lattice bound-state condition is

1/(Ct) = −(1/L³) Σ_q 1/[B + 4t Σ_i(1 − cos q_i)],

where q_i=2πm_i/L are dimensionless lattice momenta. In the infinite-volume limit at fixed lattice spacing, this becomes

1/(Ct) = −∫_[−π,π]³ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[B + 4t Σ_i(1 − cos q_i)].

This equation shows why the supplied information does not determine a numerical bare C: its value depends on the lattice cutoff, equivalently the lattice spacing, and on the corresponding t. Taking the thermodynamic limit at fixed spacing does not remove that cutoff. Taking a continuum limit also requires specifying how the bare coupling is regulated and tuned.

The regulator-independent zero-range information from the binding energy is the inverse bound-state size

κ = √(M_phy B) = √[(1634 MeV)(17.8 MeV)] ≈ 170.5 MeV,

equivalently a_s=1/κ in natural units, or a_s=ħc/κ ≈ 1.16 fm. For example, with a sharp continuum momentum cutoff Λ and relative Hamiltonian −∇²/M_phy + g₀δ³(r), the bare coupling obeys

1/g₀(Λ) = −∫_|p|<Λ d³p/(2π)³ · 1/[B+p²/M_phy]
         = −M_phy/(2π²)[Λ − κ arctan(Λ/κ)].

Thus B fixes the scattering length, not a cutoff-independent bare contact coupling.

In infinite volume the scattering states have relative energies E_rel=k²/M_phy ≥ 0. The scattering spectrum starts continuously at E=0, which is 17.8 MeV above the bound-state energy. This threshold is not a discrete, normalizable first excited state. If first excited energy is intended to mean the onset of scattering, it is the continuum threshold E=0; otherwise there is no discrete first excited level in the stated infinite-volume problem.

(e) Second excited state and degeneracy

There is no discrete second excited state, and hence no finite degeneracy for such a state, in the infinite-volume spectrum as posed. Above the bound state there is a continuum, not a sequence of isolated levels. A finite periodic box would instead have discrete levels; for zero total momentum the free relative-motion energies are E_n=(2πħc/L_phy)²|n|²/M_phy, but the contact interaction shifts these levels. Computing interacting excited levels and their degeneracies requires a specified finite box and lattice cutoff (or a fully specified renormalized finite-volume theory). Also, L→∞ at fixed lattice spacing is a thermodynamic limit, whereas a→0 at fixed physical box size is a continuum limit; they are distinct limits.
